name: Rafael Santos

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me, Rafael. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no links to companies, unions, parties or government. Everything here is confidential. To start, what does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run two five-axis CNC machines, computer-controlled milling machines, at a precision shop that makes hydraulic valve bodies for tractors and diggers. I load the aluminium blanks, set the tool offsets, start the program, and then measure the finished parts with micrometers and the measuring machine in the quality room. A good day is two hundred parts and not one scrapped. It's about forty people, family-owned, on the industrial estate by the old rail yard.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the precision, getting a bore right to a hundredth of a millimetre. What wears me out is waiting: the machine runs a forty-minute cycle and I'm just standing there, so I use that time to learn. I ask an AI assistant to explain the G-code, the instructions the machine reads, or to translate the German manual for the new spindle. My foreman Hugo calls me the professor, half as a joke.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I've got a small flat with a mortgage I'm paying down fast, and about ten months of pay saved. On weekends I rent a garage unit with an old manual mill and a 3D printer, and I make custom motorbike parts that I sell online. My girlfriend Ana is a primary school teacher, and Sunday is Mass with my parents and lunch at theirs, no exceptions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be a little disappointed. But okay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told people it was overhyped, even though I use it every day. It's a good assistant for reading manuals and checking my sums, nothing more. Online I'd post something in the motorbike forum about how it still can't design a decent exhaust bracket.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately it means my job's safe and my plans don't change. Machinists with my pay and experience are always wanted on the estate, there are four other shops within walking distance. If AI stays a fancy calculator, my real project is still the garage unit and the motorbike parts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep running the two machines and keep using AI in the cycle time to learn programming. I'd grow the motorbike parts side, maybe buy a small second-hand CNC mill for the garage for about eight thousand from my savings. And I'd keep overpaying the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit flat. I like a challenge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd buy a CNC mill with your savings. Isn't that a risk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A small one, but I've been selling the parts for two years and I know who buys them. My dad was a welder and always said a man should own his tools. If it doesn't work out, a good used mill sells for nearly what you paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Ana think of the garage business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ana supports it, but she wants weekends back once we're married. So I'd have to make it pay enough that I could hire a student on Saturdays. That's the deal we've made.

say: I'd say AI was **overhyped**, even though I use it daily.
I'd joke on the **motorbike forum** that it can't design a decent bracket.
think: My job is **safe**, with four other shops in walking distance.
My real project stays the **garage unit** and motorbike parts business.
do: Keep running **two CNC machines** and learning programming in cycle time.
Buy a **used CNC mill** for the garage for about eight thousand.
feel: **Calm**, and a little flat, because he likes a challenge.
S0.quote: If AI stays a fancy calculator, my real project is still the garage unit and the motorbike parts.
fieldNote: He is a **daily AI user** yet happily calls it overhyped in this world.
His ambition is **ownership**: owning tools and a business, as his welder father taught.
Ana sets a **clear limit** on weekend work after marriage.

steps.text: Keep running the two five-axis CNC machines
Grow online sales of custom motorbike parts
Buy a used CNC mill for the garage unit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now that one I'd like. That's the world I'm getting ready for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is good for people who learn, and hard for people who don't want to. At the shop I'd tell the younger guys to use the cycle time to learn programming, not their phones. I don't think anyone is owed a job just for turning up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it means a better job for me. The thinking side of machining, writing the programs and planning the jobs, is where AI helps most, and I already use it. I'd want to be the one who programs the machine and sets it up, not the one who loads the blanks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Hugo to let me write and prove out programs two days a week, using the AI tools to check them. I'd take an evening CAM course, that's the software that turns a drawing into machine instructions, which costs about twelve hundred. And I'd use the same tools to design motorbike parts faster for the side business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, honestly. A bit like the start of a season.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at the shop would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Old Victor, who's run the same lathe for twenty-two years and won't touch a tablet. I'd try to help him, but I can't make him want it. The office would also shrink: our quoting and buying is one woman, Sonia, and that's exactly the stuff AI does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said nobody is owed a job. Would you say that to Victor?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not in those words, no, he's like an uncle to me. I'd tell Victor the shop needs his experience to check what the machines make. But I'd still say people have to meet change halfway.

say: I'd say change rewards people who **learn** and is hard on those who won't.
I'd tell younger machinists to study **programming** in the cycle time.
think: AI helps most with the **thinking side**: programs and job planning.
I'd aim to be the one who **programs and sets up**, not loads.
do: Ask Hugo for **two days a week** writing and proving programs.
Take an evening **CAM course** costing about twelve hundred.
Use AI tools to **design bike parts** faster for the side business.
feel: **Excited**, like the start of a new season.
S1.quote: I'd want to be the one who programs the machine and sets it up, not the one who loads the blanks.
fieldNote: He sees this world as a **promotion**, moving from loading to programming.
His free-market line, nobody is **owed a job**, softens when it's Victor.
He correctly spots the **office quoting** role as most exposed in the shop.

steps.text: Ask Hugo, the foreman, for two programming days a week
Take an evening CAM software course for about twelve hundred
Design motorbike parts faster with AI tools

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Okay, that changes the maths.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the people who move now will be fine and the ones who wait will be in trouble. At Mass I'd keep it simple and say families should help each other, not wait for the government. Online I'd probably start sharing what I learn about robot cells.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, the programming job I was aiming for disappears in 2028, because AGI writes better programs than me. Then around 2031 robots load the machines, so my current job goes too. My side business also faces factories with robots, so I'd have to be cleverer than just cheap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move fast. In the first year I'd look for a job at a robot integration firm, the companies that install robot cells in shops like mine, because they'll be flat out from 2028 to 2031. I'd put about fifteen thousand of my savings into a small robot arm for the garage, to learn it on my own parts. And I'd keep the mortgage payments going but stop overpaying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but the kind of anxious that gets you up early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said integrators would be busy until 2031. What happens after?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's what keeps me up. Robot integrators will be flat out between 2028 and 2031, and after that the robots might install themselves. So maybe I get three good years and then I'm in the same boat. I'd use those three years to save hard and build the bike parts brand, because people pay for a name they trust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you talk to Ana about spending fifteen thousand on a robot arm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carefully. I'd show Ana the numbers and tell her the robot arm is a course I pay for once, not a toy. If she said no, I'd find a used one for half that.

say: I'd say people who **move now** will be fine and waiters won't.
I'd say **families** should help each other rather than wait for government.
think: The **programming job** I wanted vanishes in 2028 when AGI writes better code.
Robots load the machines by **2031**, so my current job goes too.
do: Apply to a **robot integration firm** within the first year.
Spend about **fifteen thousand** on a small robot arm for the garage.
Stop **overpaying** the mortgage to keep cash on hand.
feel: **Anxious**, but in a way that gets him up early.
S2.quote: Robot integrators will be flat out between 2028 and 2031, and after that the robots might install themselves.
fieldNote: He sees the **three-year robot lag** as a window to cash in on installing robots.
He knows the window may **close behind him** once robots can install robots.
His **free-market** instinct shows in blaming no one and planning to outrun it.
Ana is a real **check** on his spending, and he'd accept a cheaper option.

steps.text: Apply to a robot integration firm in the first year
Buy a small robot arm for the garage for about fifteen thousand
Run the garage robot arm on his own bike parts
Build the motorbike parts brand with savings from integration work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's a much more comfortable runway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to get ahead if you start now. At the shop I'd push for us to buy a robot cell before the competitors do, because the shop that waits loses the contracts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd think my shop could survive if it's early, and I could be the guy who runs its robots. AGI in 2031 takes the programming, but robots in 2034 still need someone on the floor to set up fixtures and sort out problems for a while. Five years is long enough to become that person at my own shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to Hugo and the owners with a proposal for one robot cell, and offer to lead it. I'd do a robot programming certificate, about two thousand, in the first year. And I'd buy the used CNC mill for the garage, so I have my own business ready in case the shop doesn't survive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine. A bit restless.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the owners say no to the robot cell?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd tell them politely I'm going somewhere that says yes. There are four shops on the estate and at least one of them will move early. I'd rather leave a good shop than go down with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd stay at your shop and also prepare to leave. Which is it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try to stay first, because I'm loyal to people who've treated me well. Loyalty to a good shop isn't the same as standing still, so I'd give the owners a year to decide.

say: I'd say there's time to **get ahead** if you start now.
I'd push the shop to buy a **robot cell** before competitors do.
think: My shop can survive if it's **early**, and I could run its robots.
Robots in 2034 still need someone to **set up fixtures** for a while.
do: Propose **one robot cell** to Hugo and the owners and offer to lead it.
Take a **robot programming** certificate for about two thousand.
Buy the **used CNC mill** as a fallback business.
S3.quote: Loyalty to a good shop isn't the same as standing still, so I'd give the owners a year to decide.
fieldNote: He wants to drive **automation** at his own shop rather than be its victim.
He'd give the owners **a year** before leaving for an earlier mover.
He separates **loyalty** from standing still, a theme from his traditional values.

steps.text: Propose a robot cell to the owners and offer to lead it
Earn a robot programming certificate for about two thousand
Buy a used CNC mill for the garage unit
Move to another estate shop if owners refuse after a year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's long enough to build something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift and nobody should waste it. To my friends I'd say this is when you start the business you always talked about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd think this is my chance to be an owner, not a worker. By 2036 I'd be thirty-seven, and by 2039 when robots arrive I'd want my own small shop with robots doing the loading and me selling the parts. Ten years to build a small shop with robots in it is exactly what I'd want.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd buy the used CNC mill, register the business properly and start making small batches for local shops. I'd marry Ana and we'd buy a house with room for a workshop. I'd keep my day job for at least five years so the bank sees a steady wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Honestly, a bit excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Ana say about a house with a workshop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ana would say yes to the house and no to the noise. So the workshop would be at the end of the garden, insulated properly. Her condition is that Sundays stay free, and I'd keep that promise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd worry about in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That other people use the ten years the same way, and there are too many small robot shops chasing the same tractor parts. That's why I'd build a brand in motorbike parts, where people care who made it. A robot can make a part, but it can't build trust with a customer.

say: I'd call **ten years** a gift nobody should waste.
I'd tell friends to **start the business** they always talked about.
think: This is my chance to become an **owner**, not a worker.
I'd want my own **small shop** with robots loading by 2039.
do: Buy the **used CNC mill** and register the business.
Marry Ana and buy a house with **room for a workshop**.
Keep the **day job** at least five years to reassure the bank.
S4.quote: A robot can make a part, but it can't build trust with a customer.
fieldNote: Ten years turns his worry into a **business plan** with robots working for him.
His real fear is **crowding**: too many small robot shops making the same parts.
**Family** sets the rhythm: Ana, the garden workshop and free Sundays.

steps.text: Register the business and make small batches for local shops
Buy a used CNC mill for the business
Marry Ana and buy a house with a garden workshop
Plan robot loading for his own shop by 2039

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. I'd have a plan, but it's a three-year window that could close behind me. What would help is cheap business loans for small shops buying their first robots, and fast short courses run by the firms that make them, not three-year degrees.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You could ask who will own the robots. If it's only the big companies, guys like me end up watching. If small shops and families can own the robots too, it could be the best thing that ever happened to people like my dad.

headlineQuote: If small shops and families can own the robots too, it could be the best thing that ever happened to people like my dad.
portrait: Rafael, 27, runs **two CNC machines** at a family-owned shop making hydraulic valve bodies.
He uses **AI every day**, saves about ten months of pay and runs a weekend motorbike parts business.
He is **traditional** and free-market, attends Mass with his parents and plans to marry Ana, a teacher.
He sees slow change as a **promotion** and fast change as a narrow window into robot work.
His long-term goal is **ownership**: his own small shop with robots working for him.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because his window into robot integration could close within three years.
whatWouldHelp: **Cheap business loans** for small shops buying their first robots.
Fast **short courses** run by robot makers instead of long degrees.
